excerpt: Three-way translation merge: keeping translated pages in sync with an LLM We recently rebuilt our company website. It exists in English, Swedish and Norwegian and is a static site built with Astro, with pages stored as plain MDX files in a Git repository. As with any multilingual site, you need some method to keep the translated pages in sync between languages. Due to my underlying hubris, defiant curiosity and lack of respect for existing solutions, I wanted to try an idea I’ve had for doing this. The usual way is to split each page into strings or segments and translate them one by one. Then every language has the same structure, and you correct a translation in the translation tool. I wanted each language to be a whole page that you can edit like any other page. When we edit the English page, we want the Swedish and Norwegian pages to be updated. But that’s very tedious to do by hand. And we can’t re-translate the whole page, because then we might overwrite manual corrections. What if you gave an LLM the changes made in the source page, and let it edit the existing translated page, the way a coding agent edits a file? Then it would have the context of the existing text and could perform a semantically equivalent change that wouldn’t overwrite corrected terms. The LLM would get three things: - the changes made in the source page, as a diff - the current target page - an edit tool Like this: If you use Git, you may recognize this process. When Git merges two branches, it doesn’t just compare the two versions of a file. It also looks at the last version the two branches have in common, which is called the merge base. That is a three-way merge. Git needs the base because the two versions alone don’t say who changed what. If a line is in one version and missing in the other, one side may have added it, or the other side may have removed it. With the base, Git can tell which, and it keeps the changes from both sides.
